claim: Open-source smoke detector for hilltop cameras: runs on a CPU and triangulates the fire.
data_label: real: Pyro-SDIS frames (Apache-2.0) | simulated: plumes, weather, geometry
limit: On real held-out frames the single-frame model has no skill (AUC 0.45); plume results are simulated.
alt: Top: a low-resolution hillside camera frame with a red detector box and a dashed green human label. Bottom: a map where bearing lines from two hilltop cameras cross at the estimated fire position.
post:
Forest-fire danger in Ticino, Valais and Graubuenden is a daily federal warning, but a fire that starts on a slope is still found by whoever happens to look. I built an open-source smoke detector for fixed hilltop cameras. A 410 KB model runs on a CPU in about 1 ms per frame, a background-subtraction check requires the plume to appear as change, and an alarm needs several frames in a row. The alarm threshold follows the federal forest-fire danger level, read from the public warning layer. Two cameras that see the same plume give a bearing intersection on a map.

Measured: in 40 simulated plume sequences the hybrid detector alarmed on 82 % at high danger level, with about 1.7 false-alarm episodes per camera-day on simulated clouds, fog, glare and dust. With an assumed 2 pixel bearing error the simulated two-camera fix lands a median 572 m from the fire.

Not verified: on 708 real held-out frames from unseen cameras the single-frame model has no skill (ROC AUC 0.45) because smoke is a few pixels at 160 x 96. Plumes, weather and camera geometry are simulated, so none of this is field performance. The next step is full-resolution training.

If you run camera-based fire watch: what false-alarm rate per camera-day can a duty officer actually live with?

Code: https://github.com/Usernamepersonperson/smoke-plume-camera-detector
